All pass. These reach 1227–1319 GB/s against a 1330–1372 GB/s copy ceiling — the arithmetic is fully hidden behind memory traffic. | | Activation chains with a **chained SFU dependency** (e.g. `expf` result fed straight into `log1pf`, as in softplus) | **Hard** — the dependency chain is the bottleneck | `relu`+`softplus`: 0.54×; `softplus`+`leaky_relu`: 0.57×. A single fused kernel running `expf→log1pf` measured *slower* than eager launching the same two ops as separate kernels (3503 µs vs 2110 µs). The chain gives the scheduler no independent work to overlap. PyTorch's native `softplus` takes only 1571 µs (≈400 µs over a plain copy), so it uses a fused/polynomial path not reproducible in a hand kernel. | | Reductions / convolutions / attention | **Hard wall** — cuDNN owns these | ConvTranspose1d: best hand kernel 0.34× cuDNN (4379 µs vs 1492 µs). The transpose-conv gather pattern is expensive for everyone; cuDNN is simply better. Winning needs an algorithmic rewrite (gather → GEMM + BLAS), not micro-optimization. | | **bool / int8 output** | **Deprioritize** | `flip`+`gt`: 0.29× torch.compile. Byte-strided output stores cannot coalesce on this device. Attempting to pack 4 bools into one 32-bit store segfaults — PyTorch bool tensors are 1 byte/element with no 4-byte alignment guarantee. | Rule of thumb: the win comes from **removing memory traffic**, not from writing faster arithmetic. If the op chain is memory-bound (each op is a cheap arithmetic on a full tensor), fuse it — the win is real. The exception is a **chained SFU dependency** (`exp`→`log`, `exp`→`tanh` on the same value): there the arithmetic cannot hide behind the memory traffic and even a correct fused kernel loses to eager. If it is compute-bound (reductions, library-backed ops), expect to lose to `torch.compile` or the library unless you can restate the computation. Measure, and size for the board actually visible. If a task does OOM, that is a capacity limit (`invalid_infrastructure`), not a backend bug. ### Baseline measurement caveat (important for reward integrity) The measured result must be consumed. If the return value of `forward()` is discarded, the backend eliminates the work (device-side dead code elimination) and reports a runtime that is nearly constant regardless of problem size. This is not hypothetical and it is not limited to inlined lambdas — `utils/profiling.py`'s own `benchmark_model` loop had `_ = model(*inputs)` and was affected. Measured on this stack, the discarded form understated the eager baseline by **2.3×** and the CUDA extension by **3.7×**. Because the two sides were deflated by different factors, every speedup derived from them was wrong, not merely mis-scaled: axpby at 1×128 appeared to beat torch.compile by 2.4× when the real ratio is ~1.0×. The loop now accumulates outputs into a device-side sink, which makes the numbers scale correctly with problem size. When writing your own timing code, consume the result — e.g. `sink.add_(out.sum())` — or use `out=`. ### Sizing the task At the reference example's scale (1×128) the kernel is pure launch overhead (~9 µs floor on C500) and performance differences are noise. Size tasks so kernel compute dominates: for axpby, ≥4K elements is the floor where the extension separates from baselines; ≥1M is comfortably compute/BW bound. ### Measured reference points (axpby, this host) Measured with the DCE-safe profiler (outputs consumed via a device sink): | n | eager | torch.compile | v2 kernel (float4) | v2 vs compile | |---|---|---|---|---| | 64K | 25.1 µs | 27.7 µs | 27.6 µs | 1.00× | | 1M | 49.8 µs | 50.7 µs | 51.4 µs | 0.99× | | 16M | 304.6 µs | 297.4 µs | 219.8 µs | 1.35× | Earlier runs of this same table (9.5/7.3 µs etc.) were taken with the unfixed profiler and are not real — the discarded return value let the backend eliminate most of the work. The correct picture: at 64K–1M the kernel is launch-overhead-dominated and the extension merely matches torch.compile; the win only appears once the workload is genuinely bandwidth-bound (16M). v2 (float4 vectorization) is the best of the variants tried; explicit 2-way ILP on top of it gave no further gain — the compiler already schedules it. Roofline, occupancy, and wave math remain available. ### Binding robustness (affects the reward signal) Every `*_binding.cpp` should **normalize** input dtypes rather than reject them: ```cpp if (y.dtype() != torch::kInt64) y = y.to(torch::kInt64); ``` The evaluation harness regenerates inputs with its own seed, and the dtype that arrives at `forward()` is not guaranteed to match what `get_inputs()` produced. A hard `TORCH_CHECK` on dtype yields `correctness=False` — a false negative that looks like a kernel bug but is purely a contract mismatch. Normalize, then check; never reject on dtype alone. ### Task typing: what is winnable on this device Measured across real dataset tasks on this host (KernelBench gate, `cuda_event` timing). Use this to prioritize which tasks to push on: | Task shape | Verdict | Evidence | |---|---|---| | **Memory-bound** elementwise fusion, float output (cheap ops: add/mul/relu/xor/cos/stack) | **Sweet spot** — fuse aggressively | `cos`+`stack`: 3.01× vs torch.compile; `relu`+`xor`: 1.53×. Both pass the gate with a single-pass kernel. | | Activation chains with **single-SFU or branch-free** ops (selu, tanh, log, cos, leaky_relu) | **Winnable** — fuse with float2 vectorization | G1 batch (KernelBench gate, `cuda_event`): `selu`+`tanh` 1.36×, `log`+`cos` 1.39×, `leaky_relu`×2 1.58×. All pass. These reach 1227–1319 GB/s against a 1330–1372 GB/s copy ceiling — the arithmetic is fully hidden behind memory traffic. | | Activation chains with a **chained SFU dependency** (e.g. `expf` result fed straight into `log1pf`, as in softplus) | **Hard** — the dependency chain is the bottleneck | `relu`+`softplus`: 0.54×; `softplus`+`leaky_relu`: 0.57×. A single fused kernel running `expf→log1pf` measured *slower* than eager launching the same two ops as separate kernels (3503 µs vs 2110 µs). The chain gives the scheduler no independent work to overlap. PyTorch's native `softplus` takes only 1571 µs (≈400 µs over a plain copy), so it uses a fused/polynomial path not reproducible in a hand kernel. | | Reductions / convolutions / attention | **Hard wall** — cuDNN owns these | ConvTranspose1d: best hand kernel 0.34× cuDNN (4379 µs vs 1492 µs). The transpose-conv gather pattern is expensive for everyone; cuDNN is simply better. Winning needs an algorithmic rewrite (gather → GEMM + BLAS), not micro-optimization. | | **bool / int8 output** | **Deprioritize** | `flip`+`gt`: 0.29× torch.compile. Byte-strided output stores cannot coalesce on this device. Attempting to pack 4 bools into one 32-bit store segfaults — PyTorch bool tensors are 1 byte/element with no 4-byte alignment guarantee. | Rule of thumb: the win comes from **removing memory traffic**, not from writing faster arithmetic. If the op chain is memory-bound (each op is a cheap arithmetic on a full tensor), fuse it — the win is real. The exception is a **chained SFU dependency** (`exp`→`log`, `exp`→`tanh` on the same value): there the arithmetic cannot hide behind the memory traffic and even a correct fused kernel loses to eager. If it is compute-bound (reductions, library-backed ops), expect to lose to `torch.compile` or the library unless you can restate the computation. Also note the grid granularity: a scalar kernel launching one thread per element (768K blocks × 256 threads) reached only 338–642 GB/s on this device, while the same math in `float2` with a fixed 1024-block grid-stride loop reached 1227–1319 GB/s. The C500 also ships as 16.3 GB — read the property, never infer it from the card name. Note GB vs GiB: 63.59 is the GiB figure. | 80 GB | - Any warp-level reasoning must divide by 64: `__shfl_sync` lane ranges, warp vote semantics, occupancy denominators. - Tiling windows sized for 227 KB of shared memory must be cut to ≤64 KB. - Do not assume the memory budget from the card name: the 16.3 GB variant was the reason workloads sized for 48–80 GB boards were excluded here, and on a 64 GB board that exclusion does not hold. Measure, and size for the board actually visible. If a task does OOM, that is a capacity limit (`invalid_infrastructure`), not a backend bug. ### Baseline measurement caveat (important for reward integrity) The measured result must be consumed. If the return value of `forward()` is discarded, the backend eliminates the work (device-side dead code elimination) and reports a runtime that is nearly constant regardless of problem size. This is not hypothetical and it is not limited to inlined lambdas — `utils/profiling.py`'s own `benchmark_model` loop had `_ = model(*inputs)` and was affected. Measured on this stack, the discarded form understated the eager baseline by **2.3×** and the CUDA extension by **3.7×**. Because the two sides were deflated by different factors, every speedup derived from them was wrong, not merely mis-scaled: axpby at 1×128 appeared to beat torch.compile by 2.4× when the real ratio is ~1.0×. The loop now accumulates outputs into a device-side sink, which makes the numbers scale correctly with problem size. When writing your own timing code, consume the result — e.g. `sink.add_(out.sum())` — or use `out=`. ### Sizing the task At the reference example's scale (1×128) the kernel is pure launch overhead (~9 µs floor on C500) and performance differences are noise. Size tasks so kernel compute dominates: for axpby, ≥4K elements is the floor where the extension separates from baselines; ≥1M is comfortably compute/BW bound. ### Measured reference points (axpby, this host) Measured with the DCE-safe profiler (outputs consumed via a device sink): | n | eager | torch.compile | v2 kernel (float4) | v2 vs compile | |---|---|---|---|---| | 64K | 25.1 µs | 27.7 µs | 27.6 µs | 1.00× | | 1M | 49.8 µs | 50.7 µs | 51.4 µs | 0.99× | | 16M | 304.6 µs | 297.4 µs | 219.8 µs | 1.35× | Earlier runs of this same table (9.5/7.3 µs etc.) were taken with the unfixed profiler and are not real — the discarded return value let the backend eliminate most of the work. The correct picture: at 64K–1M the kernel is launch-overhead-dominated and the extension merely matches torch.compile; the win only appears once the workload is genuinely bandwidth-bound (16M). v2 (float4 vectorization) is the best of the variants tried; explicit 2-way ILP on top of it gave no further gain — the compiler already schedules it.
